name: Arthropod-Borne and Rodent-Borne Virus Infections
aliases: Zoonotic arthropod-borne and rodent-borne viral diseases

clinicalPearls: Most arthropod-borne (arbovirus) and rodent-borne zoonotic viral infections in humans are subclinical or unrecognized; humans are usually accidental, dead-end hosts and are not important amplifiers of these viruses (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665).

Recognized illness usually falls into one of five overlapping syndromic categories: fever and myalgia (F&M), arthritis and rash (A&R), encephalitis, pulmonary disease, and viral hemorrhagic fever (VHF); a single virus may cause several of these (Harrison 22e p.1664-1665).

Fever and myalgia is by far the most common and most benign syndrome, with abrupt fever, chills, intense myalgia, malaise, anorexia, and headache with photophobia/retroorbital pain; true arthritis is absent and physical findings are minimal (Harrison 22e p.1665-1666).

A history of tick bite has more diagnostic significance than a history of mosquito exposure; clinical and epidemiologic clues may allow presumptive diagnosis in epidemics, but laboratory confirmation is required in all cases (Harrison 22e p.1664).

Arthropod vectors acquire arboviruses from viremic vertebrate blood meals; the virus must disseminate to the salivary glands (extrinsic incubation, typically 1-3 weeks in mosquitoes) before the vector can transmit; transovarial transmission to progeny is an alternative maintenance mechanism (Harrison 22e p.1664).

Rodent-borne viruses are maintained by chronically infected rodents; humans are typically infected by inhalation of or contact with aerosolized rodent excreta/secreta, and most show a high degree of rodent-virus specificity (Harrison 22e p.1664).

Lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) is acquired from the house mouse and classically causes a biphasic illness with a febrile phase followed by a CNS (meningeal) phase; patients with neuroinvasive LCM, including frank encephalitis, almost always recover fully, but the virus can cause fetal microcephaly and has been transmitted by organ transplantation (Harrison 22e p.1666-1667).

Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) begins after a 2-3 week incubation with a nonspecific 3-4 day prodrome, then rapidly progresses to noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and hypoxemic respiratory failure; coincident thrombocytopenia, circulating immunoblasts (atypical lymphocytes), and a left shift are considered almost diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.1673).

In suspected HPS, aggressive IV fluid resuscitation is hazardous because of widespread capillary leak and depressed cardiac output; management is hemodynamic/respiratory support, with ECMO for the most critically ill (Harrison 22e p.1673).

Lassa fever: most Lassa virus infections are subclinical or mild, onset is gradual (characteristic of mammarenavirus VHFs), and overt hemorrhage occurs in only about 15-30% of patients; about 30% of survivors develop sensorineural deafness (Harrison 22e p.1675-1676).

Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is the most significant VHF today, with over 100,000 severe cases annually in Asia; major agents are Hantaan (Eastern Asia), Dobrava (the Balkans), and Puumala (Europe) (Harrison 22e p.1676).

Arboviral CNS disease can leave residual deficits; spinal/motor-neuron (poliomyelitis-like) disease has been documented after West Nile virus and Japanese encephalitis virus infection, and difficulty concentrating, fatigability, tremor, and personality change are common during recovery (Harrison 22e p.1671).
harrison.pathophysiology: These taxonomically diverse zoonotic RNA viruses (Togaviridae/Alphavirus; Flaviviridae/Orthoflavivirus; the bunyaviricete families Arenaviridae, Hantaviridae, Nairoviridae, Peribunyaviridae, Phenuiviridae; Orthomyxoviridae; Bornaviridae and Rhabdoviridae; and the reovirus families) circulate in nature between arthropod vectors (mosquitoes, ticks, sandflies, midges) or chronically infected rodents and vertebrate reservoirs. Arboviruses establish chronic systemic infection of the vector after a blood meal and reach the salivary glands during extrinsic incubation (1-3 weeks in mosquitoes); vertical transovarial transmission also maintains some viruses. In arboviral encephalitis, an initial lymphoid-origin viremia seeds multifocal CNS entry, presumably via olfactory neuroepithelium/cribriform plate or brain capillary endothelium; CNS injury results partly from direct neuronal infection and partly from edema, inflammation, and host immune response, with focal neuronal necrosis, glial nodules, and perivascular lymphoid cuffing. LCM meningitis is T-cell-mediated immunopathology. VHF agents share a core pathophysiology of disrupted vascular function, stability, and integrity producing multisystem organ dysfunction and capillary leak; in HPS, widespread pulmonary capillary leak with depressed cardiac output produces noncardiogenic pulmonary edema and shock.

harrison.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on syndrome and specific virus. The F&M syndrome generally resolves completely within 2-5 days, though prolonged asthenia may follow LCMV or dengue infection. A&R illness resolves over days, but joint pain/arthritis may persist for months to years without deformity. Encephalitis ranges from full recovery (often slow, over weeks to months) to permanent deficits or death. HPS carries a case-fatality rate of approximately 30-40% even with appropriate care, though most patients surviving the first 48 hours of hospitalization recover without long-term sequelae. Argentinian and Bolivian hemorrhagic fevers can reach case-fatality rates over 50% in individual outbreaks. About 20% of Lassa virus infections become Lassa fever; survivors have roughly a 30% rate of (usually bilateral) sensorineural deafness, and pregnancy markedly worsens prognosis.
pitfalls: Anchoring on the most severe known phenotype of a virus; many agents most commonly cause mild F&M rather than their eponymous severe disease (e.g., West Nile, Venezuelan equine encephalitis, Rift Valley fever).
Treating the F&M syndrome as benign and self-limited without watching for evolution into A&R, neuroinvasive, pulmonary, or VHF syndromes for which it can be a prodrome.
Using acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) in these febrile illnesses, given the risk of exacerbated bleeding and Reye syndrome.
Giving aggressive IV fluids in HPS, which worsens noncardiogenic pulmonary edema because of capillary leak and depressed cardiac output.
Relying on a negative CSF RT-PCR to exclude arboviral encephalitis; viruses generally cannot be isolated from blood or CSF and RT-PCR cannot rule out the diagnosis.
Misreading the gradual onset of mammarenavirus VHF (Lassa, Argentinian/Bolivian) and expecting prominent early hemorrhage, which is often absent or late.
Treating a single positive heterotypic IgG cross-reaction as diagnostic in HPS serology given very low background seroprevalence.
Overlooking person-to-person/nosocomial transmission risk (Lassa virus, Andes virus, mammarenaviruses) and sexual transmission during early convalescence.
harrison.severityClassification: No single unified severity scale; severity is framed by syndrome. The five-syndrome heuristic (F&M, arthritis and rash, encephalitis, pulmonary disease, viral hemorrhagic fever) stratifies expected severity, with F&M most benign and encephalitis/pulmonary/VHF most severe. Encephalitis severity grades clinically from asymptomatic through febrile headache and aseptic meningitis to full encephalitis with coma. HPS is staged by progression from nonspecific prodrome to the cardiopulmonary phase with respiratory failure and shock. Lassa fever severity/fatality is predicted by high viral load, high serum creatinine and AST, leukocytosis, thrombocytopenia, CNS features, face/neck swelling, hypotension, hemorrhage, jaundice, and pregnancy.
management: Predominantly supportive care, with fluid and electrolyte management, antipyretics and analgesia, and organ support as required
Ribavirin for specific arenaviral and bunyaviral infections such as Lassa fever and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever where indicated
Intensive supportive care for viral haemorrhagic fever, with careful fluid balance, transfusion of blood products for coagulopathy and management of shock
Meticulous fluid management and cardiorespiratory support in hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome, with extracorporeal membrane oxygenation in refractory cases
Neurocritical care for arboviral encephalitis, including seizure control and management of raised intracranial pressure
Avoid aspirin and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs where a haemorrhagic fever such as dengue is suspected
Isolation and barrier infection-control precautions for person-to-person transmissible viruses such as Lassa and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever

Prevention through vector control, personal protective measures, avoidance of rodent-excreta exposure, vaccination where available such as against yellow fever and Japanese encephalitis, and notification to public health
